title: How to Practice Dance at Home: A Weekly Plan That Works

h1: How to practise dance at home: space, warm-up and a weekly plan
dek: A living room has no teacher, no sprung floor and no plan. Here's how to set up a safe space, warm up, structure a 30-minute session and build a week that improves you without wearing you out.

faq.q: How often should I practise dance at home?
faq.a: Three to five sessions a week of 20 to 45 minutes works for most beginners and intermediate dancers, counting classes as sessions. Beginners can start with three; add time to each session before you add more days, and keep one or two full rest days a week.

faq.q: Can I dance on a hard floor at home?
faq.a: Yes, but adapt. Tile, stone and concrete have no give, so keep jumps few and low, wear trainers or dance sneakers with grip, and avoid kneeling floor work without padding. Wood or laminate is the kindest home floor, and a roll-out dance mat or practice board gives you a studio-like surface on top.

faq.q: Should I dance in socks or barefoot at home?
faq.a: It depends on the floor. The ISTD suggests socks or soft dance shoes on carpet, bare feet or dance shoes with a grippy sole on smooth indoor floors, and shoes with grip on slippery surfaces. On carpet or rough floors, cover your skin to avoid burns.

faq.q: How long should a dance warm-up be?
faq.a: About 10 to 15 minutes. Raise your heart rate, mobilise your joints, move dynamically through your style's patterns and gently stretch, gradually. Keep long held stretches mostly for after practice.

faq.q: What should a beginner practise at home?
faq.a: Basics and posture for your style, short drills at a slow tempo, one small section of choreography until it's clean, and ten minutes of conditioning for feet, ankles and hips. Film one take per session so you can see what's actually changing.

faq.q: How do I avoid injury when practising dance at home?
faq.a: Warm up every time, clear the space, match footwear to the floor, limit jumps on hard floors, increase your practice gradually and take rest days. Most dance injuries are overuse injuries, so recovery matters. See a physiotherapist or doctor if pain is sharp, causes swelling or changes how you move.
